title: Coapt pattern-recognition myoelectric prostheses attached to transulnar osseointegration implants restore daily-living control in two patients
summary: Two transulnar amputees given Coapt pattern-recognition prostheses on osseointegration implants regained activities of daily living.
account: In an independent study funded by the Department of Veterans Affairs and published 24 December 2018, 11 users of a pattern recognition prototype that Coapt built for the DEKA Arm rated skill, comfort and weight worse than 25 users of foot-worn sensors. A JBJS Case Connector report published 15 December 2021 (Jaime, Reif, Kafedzic, Garrison, Dhawan and Rozbruch) describes two people with traumatic transulnar amputations. Both underwent osseointegration implantation. Surgery dates are not given in the abstract. After surgery a myoelectric prosthesis fitted with Coapt pattern-recognition software was attached directly to the implant. The software classifies electromyographic (EMG) signal patterns to drive a multiarticulating hand and wrist. The full case report adds that the hand fitted was a TASKA hand and that the custom implants came through a humanitarian device exemption. Both patients trained with the software. At the most recent follow-ups of 18 months and 2 years the implants showed no loosening. The authors state that prosthetic control gradually improved to allow activities of daily living. The report describes the return of activities of daily living for the first patient. For the second patient it reports two soft-tissue infections of the stoma that cleared with oral antibiotics and a flexion contracture that improved from 75 to 45 degrees.
purpose: Pattern-recognition control of a multiarticulating myoelectric hand and wrist for people with upper-limb amputation
system: Coapt pattern recognition myoelectric control (Coapt, Chicago, IL) on a multiarticulating hand and wrist
deployer: Hospital for Special Surgery, New York (Department of Limb Lengthening and Complex Reconstruction; the affiliation is given for the first author)
location: New York, New York, United States

ratings.reason: The authors report that both patients gained enough prosthetic control for activities of daily living, with the most recent follow-ups at 18 months and 2 years. The abstract gives no validated functional scores, so a lasting change is not established.
The report covers two patients at one hospital, and no source reports a realized outcome beyond them, so no societal depth can be established.

ai_role.statement: The Coapt software is a machine-learning pattern-recognition controller that maps electromyographic patterns to hand and wrist motions. The report attributes improved control to training with this software on an osseointegrated attachment. So the AI contribution is entangled with the surgical attachment and cannot be isolated.

fields.summary: Two transulnar amputees given Coapt pattern-recognition prostheses on osseointegration implants regained activities of daily living.
fields.account: In an independent study funded by the Department of Veterans Affairs and published 24 December 2018, 11 users of a pattern recognition prototype that Coapt built for the DEKA Arm rated skill, comfort and weight worse than 25 users of foot-worn sensors. A JBJS Case Connector report published 15 December 2021 (Jaime, Reif, Kafedzic, Garrison, Dhawan and Rozbruch) describes two people with traumatic transulnar amputations. Both underwent osseointegration implantation. Surgery dates are not given in the abstract. After surgery a myoelectric prosthesis fitted with Coapt pattern-recognition software was attached directly to the implant. The software classifies electromyographic (EMG) signal patterns to drive a multiarticulating hand and wrist. The full case report adds that the hand fitted was a TASKA hand and that the custom implants came through a humanitarian device exemption. Both patients trained with the software. At the most recent follow-ups of 18 months and 2 years the implants showed no loosening. The authors state that prosthetic control gradually improved to allow activities of daily living. The report describes the return of activities of daily living for the first patient. For the second patient it reports two soft-tissue infections of the stoma that cleared with oral antibiotics and a flexion contracture that improved from 75 to 45 degrees.
